idiom_name: dataclass field defaults + keyword arguments, overrides via dataclasses.replace()
implementation_notes: Python's keyword arguments and dataclass field defaults already provide the valid named base instance, and dataclasses.replace(user, email="bad@example.com") is exactly the builder's override step: a shallow copy in which only the named fields change, with the replacement going through __init__ and therefore through __post_init__ validation. A module-level factory (def a_user(**overrides)) keeps the defaults in one place, and pytest fixtures compose the same way through dependency injection for suites that prefer not to import shared helpers. Reach for the declarative factory libraries - factory_boy or polyfactory - when graphs are deep and many tests override several fields, and write a fluent builder only when construction is conditional or genuinely step-wise.
code_sketch:
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class User:
    name: str = "Ada Lovelace"
    email: str = "ada@example.com"
    age: int = 30

user = replace(User(), email="bad@example.com")  # only the asserted field
assert not can_send_invoice(user)
pitfalls: replace() copies shallowly: mutable field values (lists, dicts, nested dataclasses) are shared with the base instance unless the field's default uses field(default_factory=...) and the test replaces the whole field.
A **overrides factory silently accepts misspelled field names (a_user(emial=...)); accept typed keyword-only parameters or validate the keys, or the test runs against the defaults it meant to change.
Mutable values as class-level defaults are shared between instances; dataclasses reject a bare mutable default, but a hand-written __init__ or a module-level base instance reintroduces the leak.
